claims.claim: CoreWeave sits on the causal path from AI model demand to deployable accelerated-compute capacity by assembling scarce GPUs, energized datacenter power and cloud software into usable infrastructure; Q2 backlog near $104B and active power above 1 GW show realized demand and physical scaling rather than TAM alone.

The likely successor bottleneck is energized power and capital, not software demand: CoreWeave targets more than 8 GW by 2030 while relying on very large external financing, so compute demand can remain strong while site delivery, grid interconnection or financing constrains conversion.

Structural control is incomplete because GPUs, power and facilities are upstream dependencies and hyperscalers/other GPU clouds are substitutes; CoreWeave therefore monetizes orchestration/deployment speed more than exclusive ownership of the underlying compute bottleneck.

falsifiers: Backlog growth without proportional active-power, revenue and cash conversion would weaken the deployment-control thesis.
Sustained accelerator availability and power expansion accompanied by falling utilization/pricing would indicate demand or substitution, not supply, is the binding constraint.

risks.risk: Power/site and GPU supply can become binding successor bottlenecks even with strong AI demand.
Capital-market access is structurally coupled to expansion because infrastructure is exceptionally capital intensive.

unknowns.unknown: Exact long-run unit economics by facility and customer are not disclosed in this Beta object.

claims.claim: The strongest present challenge is financing and conversion quality, not absence of demand: CoreWeave reports roughly $104B backlog and >$30B year-to-date capital raised, while independent market lineage shows enterprise value materially above equity value and negative trailing net income.

Large backlog is not equivalent to realized economic value because recognition depends on delivery and service availability; leverage, customer concentration, GPU supply and power availability can turn schedule slippage into financing stress.

Funding access is currently a counterweight to the bear case: the August $2.6B facility and broader capital raised demonstrate continuing market access, so leverage is a material risk rather than evidence of present insolvency.

risks.risk: High leverage/capital intensity can amplify even modest deployment delays.
Backlog headline can overstate near-term economic certainty when service availability and delivery conditions remain outstanding.
Customer and supplier concentration can create correlated demand/supply shocks.

contradictions.claim: Exceptional contracted demand coexists with negative trailing earnings and heavy external financing dependence.
contradictions.resolution: Both are current facts; preserve growth evidence while carrying financing/conversion risk explicitly rather than treating backlog as cash-equivalent.

unknowns.unknown: Exact cancellation protections, customer concentration and project-level return on invested capital are not established here.
